title: Conventional Commits Format
learning_objectives: Explain the purpose and benefits of Conventional Commits specification
Identify the three required parts of a conventional commit: type, scope, description
Recognize valid commit types (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore)
Understand when to use each commit type based on the nature of changes
Differentiate between breaking and non-breaking changes in commits
Parse commit messages to extract type, scope, and description
Explain how conventional commits enable automated changelog generation
outline: Introduction: Why commit message consistency matters for CatchBook
The problem: inconsistent commit messages in real projects
Required commit types: feat and fix (semantic versioning connection)
Supporting commit types: docs, style, refactor, test, chore, perf
Understanding scope: what area of code is affected
Writing the description: imperative mood, lowercase, no period
Breaking changes: the ! syntax and BREAKING CHANGE footer
Optional commit body: explaining what and why, not how
Optional commit footer: issue references and metadata
Real-world examples from popular open-source projects
How conventional commits enable automated tools (semantic-release, changelog generation)
CatchBook commit strategy: planning our conventions
outline_structure_notes: All 14 sections are conceptual. No hands-on exercises in this lesson.
checkpoint_placement_guidance: After section 4 (anatomy), after section 8 (description rules), after section 11 (footers), after section 14 (CatchBook strategy).

catchbook_context.feature: Commit message standards for CatchBook repository
catchbook_context.deliverable: Understanding of Conventional Commits format to be applied in L02-L04

criteria: Correctly identify commit type for given code changes
Parse commit messages to extract type, scope, and description
Explain when to use each commit type (feat, fix, docs, etc.)
Articulate benefits of conventional commits for CatchBook development

professor_constraints: Use CatchBook-specific examples for all commit types (e.g., feat(auth): add user registration)
Show both good and bad commit message examples side-by-side
Emphasize that conventions reduce cognitive load over project lifetime
Connect commit types to semantic versioning (feat=minor, fix=patch, breaking=major)
Demonstrate parsing commits with regex or visual highlighting
Address common objection: 'This seems like bureaucracy' with long-term benefits
Preview how these conventions will benefit CatchBook as it grows to 28 phases
